Animals famous for long migrations.Monarch butterfly: Each autumn, monarch butterflies travel up to about 4,000 km to winter in Mexico, a trip no single butterfly makes twice.
Animals famous for long migrations.Arctic tern: The Arctic tern migrates from the Arctic to Antarctica and back, a round trip of about 70,000 km each year.
Animals famous for long migrations.Wildebeest: Over a million wildebeest follow the rains through the Serengeti and Masai Mara in the largest overland migration on Earth.
Animals famous for long migrations.Caribou: Caribou make the longest land migration of any mammal, travelling thousands of kilometres across the tundra in huge herds.
Animals famous for long migrations.Gray whale: A gray whale's yearly round trip between Alaska and Baja California can reach about 20,000 km.
Animals famous for long migrations.Humpback whale: Humpback whales feed in cold polar waters and then swim thousands of kilometres to breed in warm tropical seas.
Animals famous for long migrations.Salmon: Salmon return to the very stream where they hatched, using smell to navigate, then spawn and die.
Animals famous for long migrations.Swallow: Swallows winter in Africa and return to nest in the same barns; the saying 'one swallow doesn't make a summer' is that old.
Animals famous for long migrations.Canada goose: Canada geese fly in V-formation to save energy, and the lead bird takes turns with others.
Animals famous for long migrations.Sea turtle: Sea turtles can cross entire oceans and return to nest on the same beach where they hatched, decades later.
Animals famous for long migrations.Zebra: Zebras join the Serengeti wildebeest, and a large herd in Botswana makes the longest known mammal migration in Africa.
Animals famous for long migrations.Eel: European eels travel to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, a journey across the Atlantic of thousands of kilometres.
Animals famous for long migrations.Sloth: Sloths barely move, and a three-toed sloth descends from its tree to the ground about once a week to defecate.
Animals famous for long migrations.Koala: Koalas are homebodies; they stick to a small set of eucalyptus trees and sleep up to about 20 hours a day.
Animals famous for long migrations.Snail: Snails are famously slow, moving about one metre in an hour at best, and never go on long trips.
Animals famous for long migrations.Giant panda: Giant pandas stay in their bamboo mountains, though they may move to lower elevations when bamboo flowers and dies.
Animals famous for long migrations.Hedgehog: Hedgehogs don't migrate; they hibernate through winter, curled up in a nest of leaves.
Animals famous for long migrations.Raccoon: Raccoons stay within a small home range, usually just a few kilometres around their den.
Animals famous for long migrations.Gorilla: Gorillas live in stable family groups that roam a limited territory, and they make a new nest of leaves every night.
Animals famous for long migrations.Mole: Moles spend their lives underground in a single network of tunnels, and some can dig a tunnel up to 20 metres in a night.
Animals famous for long migrations.Hamster: Hamsters are stay-at-home creatures; wild ones live in burrows and stash food in cheek pouches that stretch to their shoulders.
Animals famous for long migrations.Platypus: The platypus stays in one stretch of Australian stream; its bill senses electric fields from prey.
Animals famous for long migrations.Chipmunk: Chipmunks are homebodies with a burrow they defend, and they stash food for winter instead of migrating.
Animals famous for long migrations.Wombat: Wombats live in burrows and don't migrate, and they use their tough rear to block tunnel entrances from predators.

Sharks.Great white: Great white sharks can detect a tiny trace of blood in the water and sometimes launch completely out of the sea when ambushing seals.
Sharks.Hammerhead: A hammerhead's wide, flat head spreads its electrical sensors, which helps it find stingrays hidden under sand, a favorite meal.
Sharks.Tiger shark: Tiger sharks eat almost anything, and stomachs examined by scientists have held tires, license plates and other odd junk.
Sharks.Whale shark: The largest fish alive, over 12 meters long, is a gentle giant that feeds mostly on plankton and tiny fish filtered from the water.
Sharks.Mako: The shortfin mako is among the fastest sharks, with bursts often estimated near 70 km/h, and it can leap several meters out of the water.
Sharks.Bull shark: Bull sharks tolerate fresh water and have been found hundreds of kilometers up rivers such as the Mississippi and the Amazon.
Sharks.Nurse shark: Nurse sharks are sluggish bottom dwellers that rest by day and hunt at night, sucking prey out of crevices like a vacuum.
Sharks.Basking shark: The second-largest fish cruises with its huge mouth open, filtering plankton, and is harmless to people despite growing past 8 meters.
Sharks.Megalodon: Megalodon was a gigantic extinct shark that vanished millions of years ago; we know it mostly from enormous fossil teeth.
Sharks.Thresher: A thresher shark's tail can be as long as its body, and it whips it to stun schools of small fish before eating them.
Sharks.Wobbegong: Wobbegongs are carpet sharks of Australasian waters; frilly whisker-like flaps and mottled skin make them nearly invisible on the reef.
Sharks.Dogfish: Dogfish are small sharks, sold in British fish shops as 'rock salmon', and the spiny dogfish carries a mild venom spine by each fin.
Sharks.Killer whale: Trap: orcas are the largest dolphins, so they're mammals rather than sharks, and they have even been recorded hunting great whites.
Sharks.Stingray: Trap: stingrays are close shark cousins with cartilage skeletons, but they're rays, a separate group of flat-bodied fish.
Sharks.Manta ray: Mantas are rays, not sharks, though they're also cartilage fish; with wingspans up to about 7 meters, they filter plankton like whale sharks.
Sharks.Sawfish: Trap: a sawfish looks like a shark with a toothed snout, but it's a ray, and it uses that saw to slash through schools of fish.
Sharks.Barracuda: Barracudas are fast, toothy bony fish, not sharks; they can strike at around 40 km/h and are often attracted to shiny objects.
Sharks.Dolphin: Dolphins are air-breathing mammals that nurse their young, and they sleep with only half of the brain at a time.
Sharks.Swordfish: Swordfish are bony fish with no teeth as adults, and they can warm their eyes and brain to hunt in cold, deep water.
Sharks.Marlin: Marlin are bony fish with spear-like bills, among the fastest in the sea, and unrelated to sharks despite the similar fin.
Sharks.Tuna: Tuna are bony fish, but some can keep their muscles warmer than the sea, a trait they share with makos and great whites.
Sharks.Moray eel: Moray eels have a second set of jaws in the throat that shoot forward to drag prey down, but they're eels, not sharks.
Sharks.Sturgeon: Sturgeon look ancient, with armor-like plates, and their eggs become caviar, but they're bony fish that lived beside the dinosaurs.
Sharks.Beluga: Beluga whales are white, chatty whales nicknamed 'canaries of the sea' for their chirps and clicks, and are not sharks.

Tree nuts.Almond: Almonds are technically the seeds of a stone fruit, relative to peaches, and sweet ones are safe whereas raw bitter ones contain cyanide precursors.
Tree nuts.Walnut: Walnuts have been eaten for thousands of years, and the Persian or English walnut is the one most often found in shops.
Tree nuts.Cashew: Cashews are always sold shelled because the shell holds a caustic oil related to the irritant in poison ivy.
Tree nuts.Pecan: Pecans are native to North America, and the name comes from an Algonquian word for nuts needing a stone to crack.
Tree nuts.Pistachio: Pistachios grow in clusters on trees, and their shells split on their own when ripe; their green color is real and natural.
Tree nuts.Hazelnut: Hazelnuts are the nut in Nutella, and Turkey grows the majority of the world's supply.
Tree nuts.Brazil nut: Brazil nuts grow on huge Amazon trees and naturally contain selenium, so just a couple a day can meet the daily need.
Tree nuts.Macadamia: Macadamia nuts are native to Australia, have one of the hardest shells of any nut, and are named after chemist John Macadam.
Tree nuts.Chestnut: Chestnuts are tree nuts that, unlike most, are low in fat and starchy, and they roast well; the American chestnut was nearly wiped out by blight.
Tree nuts.Peanut: Peanuts grow underground and are legumes, related to beans and peas, so botanically they are not tree nuts at all.
Tree nuts.Nutmeg: Nutmeg is the seed of a tropical tree, a spice not a nut, and in large doses it is actually toxic, so use it sparingly.
Tree nuts.Water chestnut: Water chestnuts are corms, the swollen stems of an aquatic plant, so they aren't nuts; their crunch stays even after cooking.
Tree nuts.Sunflower seed: Sunflower seeds are fruits of a flower head, not nuts from trees, so they don't belong to the tree nut group.
Tree nuts.Pumpkin seed: Pumpkin seeds come from a squash, not a tree, so they are not tree nuts, and they're a good source of zinc and magnesium.
Tree nuts.Chickpea: Chickpeas are legumes, not nuts, and are among the earliest crops cultivated in the Middle East.
Tree nuts.Soybean: Soybeans are legumes, not tree nuts, though roasted ones are sold as snacks called soy nuts, which is probably the source of the mix-up.
Tree nuts.Tiger nut: Tiger nuts are neither tigers nor nuts: they are small tubers of a sedge, used to make the Spanish drink horchata de chufa.
Tree nuts.Butternut squash: Butternut squash is a vegetable-fruit of the squash family, and the name merely refers to its nutty flavor.
Tree nuts.Doughnut: A doughnut contains no nut at all; the name possibly came from the small lumps of dough that early cooks fried in oil.
Tree nuts.Sesame: Sesame seeds grow in pods on a flowering plant, so they are seeds, not tree nuts, though they cause allergies similar to nuts.
Tree nuts.Flaxseed: Flaxseed is a small seed from the flax plant that gives linen, so it is no tree nut.
Tree nuts.Chia seed: Chia seeds come from a mint-family plant, so they aren't nuts, and they gave the Chia Pet its green coat.
Tree nuts.Coffee bean: Coffee beans are seeds inside a cherry-like fruit, and calling them beans is just a historical habit; they are not nuts.
Tree nuts.Lentil: Lentils are small legumes that grow in pods, so they belong with peas and beans, not with tree nuts.

Things made from almonds.Marzipan: A paste of ground almonds and sugar, shaped into fruits and figures. In Lubeck, Germany, it is a local pride.
Things made from almonds.Macaron: The colorful French sandwich cookie uses almond flour in its shells. It is not the same as the coconut macaroon.
Things made from almonds.Amaretti: Italian almond cookies. Some use bitter almonds or apricot kernels, which give their marzipan-like punch.
Things made from almonds.Frangipane: A rich almond cream used to fill tarts and pastries. It is named after an Italian nobleman's perfume, they say.
Things made from almonds.Almond milk: Ground almonds blended with water and strained. In the Middle Ages it was a common substitute for milk on fast days.
Things made from almonds.Orgeat: Sweet almond syrup with orange flower water, essential in a Mai Tai. The name comes from the French word for barley.
Things made from almonds.Turrón: Spanish nougat made with honey and toasted almonds, a Christmas tradition. It has Arabic roots and is sold in hard and soft versions.
Things made from almonds.Romesco: Catalan sauce of roasted red peppers, tomatoes and ground almonds or hazelnuts. It was a fishermen's sauce from Tarragona.
Things made from almonds.Financier: A small French almond cake made with browned butter and egg whites, baked in a mold shaped like a gold bar.
Things made from almonds.Bakewell tart: English pudding of jam and frangipane in pastry. It is named after the town of Bakewell in Derbyshire.
Things made from almonds.Ajo blanco: A chilled Spanish soup made of almonds, garlic, bread and olive oil. It is a white cousin of gazpacho, from before tomatoes arrived.
Things made from almonds.Nutella: A spread of hazelnuts and cocoa, not almonds. Hazelnuts are the primary nut, with roughly 13 percent in each jar.
Things made from almonds.Muhammara: A Syrian dip of roasted red peppers and walnuts, with pomegranate molasses. Walnuts, not almonds, give the body.
Things made from almonds.Satay sauce: Peanuts form the base of this Southeast Asian sauce. Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts.
Things made from almonds.Tahini: Sesame seed paste, a seed not a nut. It is a core ingredient of hummus and halva.
Things made from almonds.Halva: Typically sesame-based, from tahini and sugar. Some versions include nuts or pistachios but almonds are not the base.
Things made from almonds.Hummus: Chickpeas, tahini, lemon and garlic. No almonds, so it is safe for people with nut allergies, apart from tahini concerns.
Things made from almonds.Gianduja: Chocolate and hazelnut paste from Turin. Napoleon's blockade of cocoa in 1806 pushed chocolatiers to stretch it with local hazelnuts.
Things made from almonds.Peanut brittle: Peanuts set in hard caramelized sugar. Peanuts are legumes, which grow underground.
Things made from almonds.Pecan pie: A Southern American pie of pecans in a sticky syrup filling. Pecans are native to North America.
Things made from almonds.Pistachio gelato: Pistachios give it a green color, although many cheap versions use dye. The best come from Bronte in Sicily.
Things made from almonds.Cashew butter: Cashews grow hanging from a fruit called the cashew apple. The shell contains a skin-irritating oil like poison ivy.
Things made from almonds.Peanut butter: Ground roasted peanuts, not almonds. George Washington Carver promoted peanuts but did not invent peanut butter.
Things made from almonds.Coconut milk: Squeezed from coconut flesh. The coconut is a drupe, a fruit with a hard pit, so almonds are close relatives of peaches while coconuts are not.

Rivers of Africa.Nile: The longest river in the world at about 6,650 km; it flows north through Egypt, where nearly all of the country's people live along its banks.
Rivers of Africa.Congo: The deepest river in the world, at over 200 m, and the second-largest by flow. It crosses the equator twice.
Rivers of Africa.Niger: Africa's third-longest river, with a famous boomerang-shaped bend. It supports life along the edge of the Sahara in Mali, Niger and Nigeria.
Rivers of Africa.Zambezi: Home of Victoria Falls, which the Kololo people called 'smoke that thunders'. It flows through six countries to the Indian Ocean.
Rivers of Africa.Limpopo: A southern African river forming the border between South Africa and Zimbabwe. Its basin includes Kruger National Park's northern edge.
Rivers of Africa.Orange: Southern Africa's longest river, named for the Dutch House of Orange, not for the fruit. It flows through Namibia and South Africa to the Atlantic.
Rivers of Africa.Senegal: A West African river forming part of Senegal's border with Mauritania, and the country takes its name from the river.
Rivers of Africa.Okavango: A river that never reaches the sea. It spreads into a giant inland delta in Botswana's Kalahari desert, after flooding every year.
Rivers of Africa.Gambia: A small West African river, and the country of the same name is built around it, a narrow nation about 50 km wide.
Rivers of Africa.Ubangi: A Congo tributary forming part of the border between the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Republic of Congo, and the Central African Republic.
Rivers of Africa.Amazon: A trap: it is the world's largest river by volume, but flows through South America, not Africa.
Rivers of Africa.Danube: A trap: Europe's second-longest river, passing through ten countries and four capitals. Not an African river.
Rivers of Africa.Volga: A trap: Europe's longest river, flowing through Russia to the Caspian Sea. It is not African.
Rivers of Africa.Ganges: A trap: India's sacred river, where millions bathe at festivals such as the Kumbh Mela. It is Asian, not African.
Rivers of Africa.Mekong: A trap: it runs from Tibet through six Southeast Asian countries to Vietnam, so it is Asian, not African.
Rivers of Africa.Thames: A trap: London's river is only about 346 km long, which makes it a short English river, far from Africa.
Rivers of Africa.Tigris: A trap: with the Euphrates, it cradled Mesopotamia in modern Iraq, so it is an Asian river, not an African one.
Rivers of Africa.Euphrates: A trap: the Tigris's partner in ancient Mesopotamia, and the longest river in western Asia. It is not African.
Rivers of Africa.Jordan: A trap: a small Middle Eastern river famous as the site of Jesus's baptism. It is Asian, not African.
Rivers of Africa.Indus: A river flowing from Tibet to Pakistan, home of the ancient civilisation Indus Valley. Asian.
Rivers of Africa.Yangtze: A trap: Asia's longest river, at over 6,000 km, flowing across China. It is not an African river.
Rivers of Africa.Rhine: A trap: a major European river that runs from the Swiss Alps to the North Sea, so it is not African.
Rivers of Africa.Mississippi: North America's great river, whose name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning 'great river'. American.
Rivers of Africa.Murray: A trap: Australia's longest river, in the southeast, and part of the Murray-Darling system. It is not African.

Flags with a cross.Sweden: Its yellow Nordic cross on blue is modeled on Denmark's flag. The colors come from the national coat of arms, three gold crowns on blue.
Flags with a cross.Norway: A blue cross fringed in white on red, in use since 1821. Its colors match the French, British and American flags, a nod to liberty.
Flags with a cross.Denmark: The Dannebrog is the oldest continuously used national flag. Legend says it fell from the sky in 1219 during a battle in Estonia.
Flags with a cross.Finland: The blue cross on white stands for the country's lakes and snow, and the flag was adopted in 1918 after independence from Russia.
Flags with a cross.Iceland: A red cross edged with white on blue. The design is based on the Nordic cross, and its colors represent fire, ice and the ocean.
Flags with a cross.Switzerland: One of only two square national flags, along with Vatican City's. The white cross on red inspired the Red Cross emblem, which reverses the colors.
Flags with a cross.United Kingdom: The Union Flag merges the crosses of St. George, St. Andrew and St. Patrick. It's not symmetrical, so it often gets hung upside down by mistake.
Flags with a cross.Greece: A white cross sits in the corner of blue and white stripes. The nine stripes are said to match the syllables of a Greek freedom slogan.
Flags with a cross.Georgia: Its flag has a large red cross with four smaller crosses, called the Five Cross Flag. The design is linked to medieval Georgia and the crusades.
Flags with a cross.Tonga: The red cross on a white canton, with a red field, is based on the Christian faith. It has been used since the mid-19th century.
Flags with a cross.Dominican Republic: A white cross divides the blue and red quarters. It's the only flag to show a Bible open in its coat of arms at the center.
Flags with a cross.Germany: The black, red and gold bands carry no cross. Its colors trace to a 19th-century nationalist movement, and they returned after 1949.
Flags with a cross.France: The blue, white and red tricolor holds no cross. It was born in the French Revolution and has inspired many flags worldwide.
Flags with a cross.Italy: Its green, white and red vertical bands carry no cross. The design copied the French tricolor brought by Napoleon's armies.
Flags with a cross.Japan: It shows just a red disc on a white field and has no cross. The simple design is among the most recognizable flags in the world.
Flags with a cross.Canada: The red maple leaf flag has no cross, though the old Red Ensign carried a Union Jack. It was replaced in 1965.
Flags with a cross.Austria: Red, white, red horizontal bands, with no cross. It's among the world's oldest flags, supposedly stained with blood on a duke's tunic in 1191.
Flags with a cross.Poland: Plain white and red horizontal stripes without a cross. The flag has the same colors as Poland's old coat of arms, a white eagle on red.
Flags with a cross.Netherlands: Red, white and blue horizontal stripes with no cross. It began as orange, white and blue, the colors of William of Orange.
Flags with a cross.Estonia: Its blue, black and white stripes carry no cross. Blue stands for sky and sea, black for the soil, and white for snow and the struggle for freedom.
Flags with a cross.Belgium: Black, yellow and red vertical bands carry no cross. The colors come from the arms of the Duchy of Brabant.
Flags with a cross.Ireland: The green, white and orange tricolor holds no cross, though St. Patrick's saltire exists as a separate symbol. White stands for peace.
Flags with a cross.Turkey: Its red flag shows a white crescent and star, with no cross. It's a symbol used by Ottomans, even though Christianity's cross has never featured.
Flags with a cross.Spain: Red and yellow stripes with a coat of arms but no cross in the design. The arms hold pillars with a motto about going further.

Flags with a crescent moon.Turkey: The white crescent and star on a red field is the national flag, called Ay Yıldız. The crescent became linked to the Ottoman Empire.
Flags with a crescent moon.Pakistan: A white crescent and star on dark green, with a white stripe. The crescent stands for progress and the star for light and knowledge.
Flags with a crescent moon.Algeria: Its green and white flag carries a red crescent and star. Red is rare for the crescent, as most flags use white or gold.
Flags with a crescent moon.Tunisia: The red flag has a white disc with a red crescent and star. It looks much like Turkey's flag because of shared Ottoman history.
Flags with a crescent moon.Malaysia: The crescent and 14-pointed star sit in the corner of 14 red and white stripes, and the points stand for the states and federal territories.
Flags with a crescent moon.Singapore: A white crescent and five stars on red stands for a young, rising nation. The five stars represent democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality.
Flags with a crescent moon.Maldives: A green rectangle bears a white crescent on a red field. It's one of the few flags that shows only a crescent without a star.
Flags with a crescent moon.Libya: The current flag with a white crescent and star on black came back in 2011 after the Gaddafi era, when the flag had been plain green.
Flags with a crescent moon.Mauritania: A yellow crescent and star on green, with red stripes added in 2017 to honor those who died fighting for independence.
Flags with a crescent moon.Azerbaijan: The crescent and an eight-pointed star in the middle sit on three bands of blue, red and green. The colors stand for Turkic heritage, modernity and Islam.
Flags with a crescent moon.Uzbekistan: Its flag has a white crescent and twelve stars on blue, over white and green stripes. The stars may stand for months or the zodiac.
Flags with a crescent moon.Turkmenistan: Its green flag has a white crescent with five stars beside a carpet-pattern stripe. The stars represent the country's five traditional regions.
Flags with a crescent moon.Saudi Arabia: The green flag bears the Islamic creed and a sword, not a crescent. The creed is sacred, so the flag is never flown at half-mast.
Flags with a crescent moon.Egypt: Red, white and black bands with the golden Eagle of Saladin in the center. There's no crescent despite the country's strong Islamic heritage.
Flags with a crescent moon.Morocco: A green five-pointed star, the Seal of Solomon, sits on a red field. No crescent features on the flag.
Flags with a crescent moon.Iran: Green, white and red bands with an emblem in the center. It's a stylized form of the word Allah, and it contains no crescent.
Flags with a crescent moon.Iraq: Its flag has red, white and black bands with the takbir in green script. The words say God is great, and no crescent is used.
Flags with a crescent moon.Jordan: Its flag has black, white and green bands with a red triangle and a white seven-pointed star. No crescent is used.
Flags with a crescent moon.Indonesia: Just red over white. Monaco's flag is nearly identical, and neither has a crescent despite Indonesia's Muslim majority.
Flags with a crescent moon.Bangladesh: A red disc on deep green, and the disc is the rising sun. It's often mistaken for Japan's flag, but there is no crescent.
Flags with a crescent moon.Israel: Its flag shows a blue Star of David on white with two blue stripes, based on a prayer shawl. It has no crescent.
Flags with a crescent moon.Japan: A plain red sun disc on white, the Hinomaru. The sun, not the moon, is its entire theme, so no crescent here.
Flags with a crescent moon.Lebanon: A green cedar tree sits on a white band between two red stripes. There's no crescent, only the cedar, an ancient symbol of the land.
Flags with a crescent moon.Oman: White, red and green bands with a national emblem of a dagger and crossed swords in the corner. No crescent appears.

Landforms (not weather).Mesa: Spanish for table, a flat-topped landform with steep sides, common in the American Southwest.
Landforms (not weather).Butte: A steep-sided, flat-topped hill that is taller than it is wide, as in Monument Valley, and the name is French for small hill.
Landforms (not weather).Delta: Named after the Greek letter, because Herodotus noted that the Nile's mouth had that triangular shape.
Landforms (not weather).Canyon: The Grand Canyon is about 446 km long and up to 1.8 km deep, and was carved by the Colorado River.
Landforms (not weather).Isthmus: A narrow strip of land between two seas, like Panama, which links North and South America.
Landforms (not weather).Atoll: A ring-shaped coral reef around a lagoon. Darwin explained that they form around sunken volcanoes.
Landforms (not weather).Plateau: A high, flat area, like Tibet's, often called the roof of the world.
Landforms (not weather).Gorge: A narrow valley with steep walls, often carved by a river over millions of years.
Landforms (not weather).Moraine: A ridge of rocks and debris dropped by a glacier, such as Long Island, which is a moraine.
Landforms (not weather).Dune: Large sand dunes can produce a low booming sound, which are called singing dunes.
Landforms (not weather).Escarpment: A long steep slope or cliff separating two levels of land, such as the Niagara Escarpment.
Landforms (not weather).Valley: A low area between hills, often carved by a river or glacier.
Landforms (not weather).Peninsula: Land surrounded by water on three sides, from Latin for almost island.
Landforms (not weather).Monsoon: A seasonal wind shift that brings heavy rain, and its name comes from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season, so it is weather.
Landforms (not weather).Tornado: A rotating column of air that can reach 300 miles an hour winds, so this is weather, not land.
Landforms (not weather).Drizzle: Very fine rain with tiny drops, which is weather.
Landforms (not weather).Blizzard: Heavy snow with strong wind and low visibility, so it is weather.
Landforms (not weather).Hurricane: A tropical storm, weather by definition, and the same system is a typhoon or cyclone elsewhere.
Landforms (not weather).Cyclone: A storm system with rotating winds, so weather.
Landforms (not weather).Sleet: Freezing rain or partly melted snow, so weather.
Landforms (not weather).Hail: Balls of ice that grow inside storm clouds, so it is weather.
Landforms (not weather).Typhoon: The name for a hurricane in the north-west Pacific, so it is weather.
Landforms (not weather).Squall: A sudden, brief burst of wind, often with rain, so it is weather.
Landforms (not weather).Fog: A cloud at ground level, so it is weather rather than a landform.

Fruits (botanically speaking).Tomato: A berry, in botanical terms. In 1893, the US Supreme Court ruled it a vegetable for tariff purposes anyway.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Cucumber: A fruit, since it develops from a flower and holds seeds. It is about 95 percent water.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Pumpkin: Botanically a fruit, in fact a type of berry. The giant ones have weighed over 1,000 kilograms.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Eggplant: A berry, relative of the tomato and potato. The name comes from some early varieties that were small, white and egg-shaped.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Bell pepper: A fruit that develops from a flower and carries seeds. Green, yellow and red can be one plant at different stages of ripeness.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Avocado: A fruit with a single large seed, so it's a berry in botany. It is one of the few fruits rich in fat.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Olive: A fruit with one stone, called a drupe, like a peach. Raw olives are very bitter and have to be cured before they can be eaten.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Zucchini: Often cooked like a vegetable, but it is the immature fruit of a squash plant, with seeds inside. Its flowers are edible.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Okra: The edible pods are fruits full of seeds. Its slimy texture is used to thicken gumbo.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Chili pepper: A fruit whose heat comes from capsaicin, which birds can't feel. That way, birds spread the seeds, while mammals avoid them.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Green bean: The pod is the fruit of a bean plant, and the beans inside are its seeds. It's one of many 'vegetables' that are botanical fruits.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Strawberry: A trap: it's not a true berry. The seeds on the outside are the actual fruits, and the red flesh is swollen flower base.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Corn kernel: Each kernel is a fruit, called a grain or caryopsis. A single ear has hundreds of kernels, each from its own silk strand.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Carrot: A root, not a fruit, as it develops underground without seeds. Carrots were originally purple or white, and orange ones were bred in the Netherlands.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Potato: A tuber, a swollen underground stem. The little green fruits that sometimes grow on the plant are poisonous.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Celery: The part you eat is the leaf stalk, not a fruit. It's mostly water, and the seeds are used as a spice.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Lettuce: A leaf vegetable. Lettuce belongs to the daisy family, with relatives like sunflowers.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Onion: A bulb, made of layers of leaf bases. Its chemical defenses make you cry when cut.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Rhubarb: In 1947 a New York court ruled it a fruit for customs purposes, but botanically you eat a leaf stalk. The leaves are poisonous.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Broccoli: The part you eat is the plant's flower buds, not the fruit. Broccoli, cabbage and kale are all the same species, bred differently.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Cauliflower: A cluster of undeveloped flower buds, not fruit. It's the same species as broccoli and cabbage.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Spinach: Its reputation as an iron powerhouse is exaggerated. It has some iron, but far less than legend says, and it is not absorbed easily.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Asparagus: The edible spears are young shoots, not fruits. A plant can keep producing for 15 to 20 years.
Fruits (botanically speaking).Ginger: A rhizome, an underground stem, not a fruit. It's a close relative of turmeric and cardamom.

Characters from The Office (US).Michael Scott: The regional manager's 'World's Best Boss' mug is no accident: Steve Carell improvised many of his most cringeworthy lines.
Characters from The Office (US).Dwight Schrute: Dwight runs a beet farm on the side and acts as a volunteer sheriff's deputy. Rainn Wilson's character also has a Schrute Farms bed-and-breakfast.
Characters from The Office (US).Jim Halpert: Jim's classic prank is putting Dwight's stapler in Jell-O. John Krasinski later went on to direct the horror hit A Quiet Place.
Characters from The Office (US).Pam Beesly: Pam starts as the receptionist and becomes a salesperson and artist. Jenna Fischer has said she worked as a real receptionist for the show's pilot.
Characters from The Office (US).Kevin Malone: Kevin famously spills his giant pot of chili in one episode. Actor Brian Baumgartner is a real chili fan and has shared the recipe.
Characters from The Office (US).Angela Martin: The uptight accountant is obsessed with cats, and her feline Sprinkles became a running gag after a rather sad office moment.
Characters from The Office (US).Oscar Martinez: Oscar is the sharp-minded accountant who is gay, and played by Oscar Nunez, one of the first openly gay office characters on mainstream sitcoms.
Characters from The Office (US).Stanley Hudson: Stanley is the grumpy salesman who loves crossword puzzles, and 'Did I stutter?' became one of his best-known lines.
Characters from The Office (US).Creed Bratton: Creed Bratton plays a character with his own name, and the real Creed was once the guitarist of the 1960s rock band The Grass Roots.
Characters from The Office (US).Toby Flenderson: Toby is Michael's hated HR rep, and Paul Lieberstein, who plays him, also served as a writer and showrunner for the show.
Characters from The Office (US).Ryan Howard: Ryan starts as a temp and later rises to corporate. B.J. Novak, who plays him, was also a writer and producer on the show.
Characters from The Office (US).Kelly Kapoor: Kelly is the gossip-obsessed customer service rep, played by Mindy Kaling, who also wrote many of the show's episodes.
Characters from The Office (US).Andy Bernard: Andy loves a cappella and calls himself 'Nard Dog'. Ed Helms, who plays him, is a real banjo player.
Characters from The Office (US).Leslie Knope: Leslie is the Parks and Recreation optimist. The show shares The Office's mockumentary style but is set in Pawnee, Indiana.
Characters from The Office (US).Ron Swanson: Ron is the mustached boss on Parks and Recreation, played by Nick Offerman, who is a real-life woodworker and has a woodshop.
Characters from The Office (US).April Ludgate: April is the deadpan intern in Parks and Recreation, and Aubrey Plaza's sarcastic style defines her, not Dunder Mifflin.
Characters from The Office (US).Tom Haverford: Tom is an entrepreneur with big schemes in Parks and Recreation, played by Aziz Ansari, and he isn't a Scranton salesman.
Characters from The Office (US).Jake Peralta: Jake is the immature detective from Brooklyn Nine-Nine, played by Andy Samberg, a cop sitcom with no paper company in sight.
Characters from The Office (US).Amy Santiago: Amy is a by-the-book detective in Brooklyn Nine-Nine, played by Melissa Fumero, and she is not at Dunder Mifflin.
Characters from The Office (US).Ted Mosby: Ted narrates How I Met Your Mother to his kids, so he belongs to that sitcom, not to Scranton's paper company.
Characters from The Office (US).Liz Lemon: Tina Fey created and played head writer Liz Lemon in 30 Rock, a show inspired by her years at Saturday Night Live.
Characters from The Office (US).Jack Donaghy: Alec Baldwin's network executive from 30 Rock is a different sitcom, and he's a Republican-leaning boss who loves his NBC job.
Characters from The Office (US).Chidi Anagonye: Chidi is the ethics professor from The Good Place, who is so indecisive that his indecision becomes a joke, and not an office worker.
Characters from The Office (US).Abed Nadir: Abed is the film-obsessed student of Community, played by Danny Pudi, who attends Greendale rather than working at Dunder Mifflin.

Addams Family characters.Gomez: John Astin played Gomez in the 1964 sitcom, and Raul Julia made him dashing in the 1991 film.
Addams Family characters.Morticia: Carolyn Jones played Morticia on TV, and Anjelica Huston took the role in the 1991 film.
Addams Family characters.Wednesday: Charles Addams's cartoon family had no names until the TV show, which named her after the 'Wednesday's child is full of woe' rhyme.
Addams Family characters.Pugsley: Pugsley is Wednesday's brother, who loves explosives and his pet octopus Aristotle.
Addams Family characters.Uncle Fester: Fester can light a bulb in his mouth, and Jackie Coogan, who played him, was a child star in Chaplin's The Kid.
Addams Family characters.Lurch: The towering butler, played by Ted Cassidy, drawled 'You rang?' and could play the harpsichord.
Addams Family characters.Thing: Thing is a disembodied hand, and on the 1960s show it was often played by Ted Cassidy, who also played Lurch.
Addams Family characters.Grandmama: Grandmama, the family's potion-brewing witch, is a key part of the clan.
Addams Family characters.Cousin Itt: Cousin Itt, covered head to toe in hair and speaking in high-pitched gibberish, was played by Felix Silla in the 1960s.
Addams Family characters.Herman Munster: Herman is the Frankenstein-like father of The Munsters, which premiered in 1964, the same year as The Addams Family.
Addams Family characters.Lily Munster: Lily is Herman's vampire wife on The Munsters, a rival monster family from the same TV season.
Addams Family characters.Eddie Munster: Eddie is a werewolf boy with a widow's peak, and he belongs to the Munsters.
Addams Family characters.Marilyn Munster: Marilyn is the 'normal' niece of the Munsters who's the family's odd one out.
Addams Family characters.Beetlejuice: Beetlejuice is a ghost from Tim Burton's 1988 film who is summoned by saying his name three times.
Addams Family characters.Lydia Deetz: Winona Ryder's goth teen Lydia sees ghosts in Beetlejuice, a different spooky family from the Addamses.
Addams Family characters.Casper: Casper the Friendly Ghost debuted in a 1939 children's story and Paramount cartoons in the 1940s.
Addams Family characters.Jack Skellington: Jack is the pumpkin king of The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993), directed by Henry Selick.
Addams Family characters.Sally: Sally is a patchwork rag doll in The Nightmare Before Christmas, and she's in love with Jack.
Addams Family characters.Dracula: Dracula is the vampire from Bram Stoker's 1897 novel, and he belongs to Transylvania, not the Addams mansion.
Addams Family characters.Mavis: Mavis is Dracula's teen daughter in Hotel Transylvania, not an Addams.
Addams Family characters.Elvira: Elvira, Mistress of the Dark, is a horror host played by Cassandra Peterson and not an Addams relative.
Addams Family characters.Frankenstein: Frankenstein is actually the doctor, not the monster, in Mary Shelley's 1818 novel.
Addams Family characters.Sparky: Sparky is the reanimated dog of Tim Burton's Frankenweenie, not the Addams family pet.
Addams Family characters.Sabrina: Sabrina Spellman is a teenage witch from Archie Comics, which has no ties to the Addams family.

Things you'd see in a classic Western.Saloon: Western saloons were real, but swinging half-doors were more a movie staple than real fixture, helping show a quick entrance or exit.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Tumbleweed: The rolling bush is usually Russian thistle, which arrived in the US in the 1870s, and so is oddly a 'foreign' symbol of the West.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Sheriff: The real office is old, from the Anglo-Saxon 'shire reeve', an official of the English shire.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Stagecoach: John Ford's 1939 film Stagecoach made John Wayne a star and shot in Monument Valley.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Cowboy hat: The Stetson, introduced in 1865, was nicknamed the 'ten-gallon hat', though it holds far less than that.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Lasso: Cowboys' lassos came from Spanish vaqueros, and the word comes from the Spanish 'lazo'.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Spurs: Spurs often had rowels that jingled as cowboys walked, and the jangling sound became a signature of Western films.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Horse: Real cowboys spent most of their working day on horseback and they picked horses for stamina over beauty.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Cactus: The tall saguaro cactus seen in many Westerns grows only in the Sonoran Desert, so films often used it as a stand-in for any desert.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Wanted poster: Real Old West wanted posters offered rewards, and the famous 'Dead or Alive' wording was used on some, though far less than movies suggest.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Bandana: Cowboys tied bandanas over their faces against trail dust, and used them as sweat rags, so the look was practical.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Ranch: Ranches in movies are often depicted as small family places, though the biggest ranches covered thousands of acres.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Showdown: The classic noon duel is largely a movie invention; real Old West gunfights were rarely staged face-offs.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Lightsaber: It belongs to Star Wars, not the West. Though Star Wars borrowed heavily from Westerns, including Han Solo's gunslinger style.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Spaceship: Spaceships don't belong in a classic Western, though TV's Firefly mixed the two successfully.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Robot: Westworld, with robot gunslingers, mixed the genres, but classic Westerns had none.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Laser: Lasers are sci-fi, and the first working one was built in 1960, long after the Old West.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Alien: Aliens don't appear in a classic Western, but the 2011 film Cowboys & Aliens decided to combine them.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Astronaut: Space is far from the Old West, and the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin, flew in 1961, a century later.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Teleporter: A staple of Star Trek, the teleporter would have been a bit too sci-fi for the dusty trail.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Hoverboard: Back to the Future Part II popularized the hoverboard, while Part III visits the Old West.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Jetpack: Jetpacks are sci-fi gear, though real rocket belts were tested in the 1960s, a century after the Old West ended.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Starship: Starships are science fiction, a far-off frontier from the Western's dusty one, though Star Trek's pitch called it 'Wagon Train to the stars'.
Things you'd see in a classic Western.Warp drive: Faster-than-light travel is a Star Trek idea, and so doesn't suit the Western's horse-powered pace.

Animals that bark.Dog: Dogs bark mainly because of living with humans; wolves rarely do, so barking may have been bred into dogs.
Animals that bark.Seal: Seals bark loudly and clap their flippers to call, and a seal pup learns its mother's bark to find her in a crowded colony.
Animals that bark.Sea lion: California sea lions are famous for their loud barks, and unlike seals they can rotate their rear flippers forward to walk on land.
Animals that bark.Fox: Foxes can make dozens of sounds, including a short sharp bark used to warn other foxes, and a scream that can sound human.
Animals that bark.Deer: A startled deer barks a harsh warning to alert the herd, and muntjac are even nicknamed barking deer.
Animals that bark.Prairie dog: Their name comes from their dog-like yips, and scientists found they use different calls to describe a predator's size, shape and colour.
Animals that bark.Baboon: Males give a sharp two-note bark as an alarm when predators such as leopards come near the troop.
Animals that bark.Squirrel: Squirrels bark when they spot a threat and can flick their tails along with the sound to warn others.
Animals that bark.Coyote: Its scientific name means "barking dog", and it is known for yips, barks and howls that sound like many more animals.
Animals that bark.Cat: Cats meow mainly to talk to humans, rarely to each other, and do not bark.
Animals that bark.Horse: A horse neighs and whinnies, and it can sleep standing up thanks to a locking mechanism in its legs.
Animals that bark.Cow: A cow moos, and it has four stomach compartments, though technically it has one stomach with four chambers.
Animals that bark.Sheep: Sheep bleat, and they can recognise at least 50 sheep faces and remember them for years.
Animals that bark.Duck: A duck quacks, and the old claim that a duck's quack doesn't echo is a myth.
Animals that bark.Owl: Owls hoot rather than bark, and they can turn their heads about 270 degrees.
Animals that bark.Snake: Snakes hiss, and they sense vibrations through their jaws as they have no external ears.
Animals that bark.Pig: A pig grunts and squeals, and pigs are often rated as smarter than dogs in tests.
Animals that bark.Goat: A goat bleats, and goats have rectangular pupils that give them a wide field of vision.
Animals that bark.Lion: A lion roars, and the sound can be heard from about five miles away.
Animals that bark.Elephant: An elephant trumpets and also rumbles at frequencies too low for humans to hear.
Animals that bark.Frog: Frogs croak, and some tree frogs can freeze solid in winter and thaw out alive.
Animals that bark.Rabbit: A rabbit is almost silent, but it thumps its hind foot to warn others, and screams if in extreme distress.
Animals that bark.Goose: Geese honk, and they fly in V formations that save energy by riding the lead bird's air.
Animals that bark.Mouse: Mice squeak, and they also sing ultrasonic songs that humans cannot hear.

American football terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is worth six points, and the name is odd because the ball no longer has to touch the ground.
American football terms.Field goal: A field goal is a kick worth three points, and the longest in the NFL, 66 yards, was kicked by Justin Tucker in 2021.
American football terms.Quarterback: The quarterback is the leader of the offense, and every play passes through his hands with the center's snap.
American football terms.Sack: A sack is tackling the quarterback behind the line, and the stat was not officially recorded by the NFL until 1982.
American football terms.Fumble: A fumble is a lost grip on the ball, and whoever recovers it can score if they run it back.
American football terms.Interception: An interception is a pass caught by the defense, and the player can run it back for a touchdown, called a pick-six.
American football terms.End zone: The end zone is the 10-yard strip behind each goal line, and a ball carrier scores by breaking the plane of its front edge.
American football terms.Huddle: The huddle is credited to Paul Hubbard, a deaf Gallaudet quarterback, who gathered teammates in 1894 so rivals couldn't see his signs.
American football terms.Punt: A punt is a kick dropped from the hands to give the ball to the other team deep in their territory.
American football terms.Blitz: A blitz sends extra defenders after the quarterback, and the word is short for the German Blitzkrieg.
American football terms.First down: A first down is a new set of four tries to gain 10 yards, and it is why the chains and the first-down line exist.
American football terms.Hail Mary: A Hail Mary is a long, desperate pass at the end of a game, and Roger Staubach named it after a 1975 playoff win.
American football terms.Linebacker: The linebacker lines up behind the line, tackles runners and chases the passer, and it's one of football's most physically demanding roles.
American football terms.Home run: A home run is baseball's, and football's long run to the end zone is simply a touchdown, whether it covers a yard or 99.
American football terms.Scrum: A scrum is rugby's restart, but football's line of scrimmage is a descendant of it: Walter Camp replaced the scrum with a line in 1880.
American football terms.Lineout: A lineout is a rugby restart in which teammates lift a jumper to catch a throw from the sideline; football has no such throw-in.
American football terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's, and football's closest thing is the Y-shaped goalpost, which a field goal kick must clear above the crossbar.
American football terms.Hat trick: A hat trick, three goals in one game, began in cricket; three touchdowns by one player is just a very big day in football.
American football terms.Birdie: Birdie is golf's one under par, and football's birds are only the mascots, such as the Eagles, Ravens and Falcons.
American football terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is basketball's; a football player dunking over the crossbar was banned for years, until the NFL relaxed it in 2014.
American football terms.Free throw: A free throw is basketball's unguarded shot after a foul; football's penalties instead move the ball by yards.
American football terms.Deuce: Deuce is tennis's 40-all, and football settles ties with overtime, which the NFL's regular season limits to 10 minutes.
American football terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess's final move; football's chess match is the playbook, and some teams carry hundreds of plays.
American football terms.Puck: A puck is ice hockey's hard rubber disc, which is flat unlike football's pointed prolate ball.

Properties on the US Monopoly board.Boardwalk: The priciest square on the board at $400, named for the famous Atlantic City boardwalk that inspired the whole map.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Park Place: Park Place costs $350, the second-priciest street and the dark blue partner of Boardwalk, so the pair is the board's most dangerous set.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Baltic Avenue: Baltic Avenue is one of the two cheapest streets at $60. The brown pair is mostly a trap for newcomers.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Mediterranean Avenue: Mediterranean Avenue costs $60 and is the first property after Go. All the streets are real roads in Atlantic City, New Jersey.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Marvin Gardens: Marvin Gardens is a misspelling of Marven Gardens, a neighbourhood in nearby Margate City. Parker Brothers never corrected it.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Illinois Avenue: Illinois Avenue is the red set's top property at $240, and in strategy surveys it is one of the most-landed-on squares.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Atlantic Avenue: The first of the yellow set at $260. The board is a map of Atlantic City, New Jersey, and this street shares its name with the ocean.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Reading Railroad: The Reading Railroad is pronounced 'Redding', after the Pennsylvania city. Owning all four railroads earns rent of $200 per turn.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Pennsylvania Avenue: A $320 green property named for an Atlantic City street, not the Washington avenue that leads to the White House.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Ventnor Avenue: Ventnor Avenue is the yellow set's second property. It lies in Ventnor City, just southwest of Atlantic City.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.St. James Place: St. James Place is orange, $180. The set of oranges is, statistically, the best to own because of the jail's position.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Oriental Avenue: Oriental Avenue is a $100 light blue, just after the Reading Railroad, and the street is part of Atlantic City's real grid.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Kentucky Avenue: Kentucky Avenue is red at $220, and it is often landed on after leaving Jail since red is the hot zone.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.B&O Railroad: The B&O Railroad stands for the Baltimore and Ohio, America's first common-carrier railroad, founded in 1827.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Mayfair: Mayfair is the most expensive property in the UK edition, not the US one, where Boardwalk plays that role.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Park Lane: Park Lane is the UK partner of Mayfair, so the US board has no such street.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Old Kent Road: Old Kent Road is the UK's cheapest square, equivalent to Mediterranean Avenue, and part of the British-only set.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Fifth Avenue: Fifth Avenue is not on the standard US board, though it appears in New York-themed editions.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Wall Street: Wall Street isn't on the classic board; it only turns up in later themed versions.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Broadway: Broadway is not in the classic US game. It appears in Monopoly Here and Now.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Rodeo Drive: Rodeo Drive is not on the original board, which draws only on streets from Atlantic City.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Lombard Street: Lombard Street is not on the US board, though it is a real San Francisco icon and a London street too.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Sunset Boulevard: Sunset Boulevard appears in some city editions but not in the classic Atlantic City version.
Properties on the US Monopoly board.Times Square: Times Square is not on the classic board, but it does appear in some themed editions.

Medieval weapons.Longbow: A Welsh and English weapon up to 2 m tall, with a draw weight of 100 pounds or more, that decided Crécy in 1346 and Agincourt in 1415. Archers trained from boyhood.
Medieval weapons.Crossbow: Easier to learn than the longbow, which made it a threat to knights. A pope tried to ban its use against Christians in 1139.
Medieval weapons.Mace: A club with a heavy metal head, good at dinting plate armour and cracking helmets. Later it became the symbol of authority in parliaments.
Medieval weapons.Flail: A spiked ball on a chain, though it's mostly a peasant's tool for threshing grain. It is often seen in fiction more than in real medieval fighting.
Medieval weapons.Halberd: A long pole topped with an axe blade and spike. Its hook could drag a knight off his horse, and the Swiss used it with devastating effect.
Medieval weapons.Lance: The knight's main charging weapon, held couched under the arm. A cavalry charge's impact came from the horse's momentum, not the arm.
Medieval weapons.Broadsword: The knight's cross-hilted double-edged sword. It was used for cutting, and was lighter than many people think, about 1.1 to 1.4 kg.
Medieval weapons.Battle axe: A practical weapon that could split shields and armour. The Vikings favoured the broad Dane axe, a two-handed model.
Medieval weapons.Trebuchet: A siege engine of counterweights that could hurl rocks of 100 kg or more over castle walls. Some versions could fling fireballs or diseased animals.
Medieval weapons.Morning star: A mace with spikes, though the name is also used for a spiked-ball-on-a-chain type. It was cheap, simple, and brutally effective.
Medieval weapons.Pike: A spear up to 5 m long, used in tight blocks by Swiss and later Landsknecht troops to stop cavalry.
Medieval weapons.War hammer: One side a hammer head, the other a spike. It was made to pierce plate armour, where swords bounced off.
Medieval weapons.Rifle: A gun with spiralled barrel grooves that improve accuracy. These were common only after the Middle Ages.
Medieval weapons.Grenade: The hand-thrown explosive spread in the 1600s, well after medieval times. Early ones were iron balls filled with gunpowder.
Medieval weapons.Bazooka: A 20th-century anti-tank rocket launcher, first used in WWII in 1942. Its name came from a comic musical instrument.
Medieval weapons.Tank: The first tanks, in 1916, were British. The name came from a cover story that they were water tanks.
Medieval weapons.Revolver: The revolver appeared in the 1800s, after the Middle Ages. Its rotating cylinder was a new idea then.
Medieval weapons.Machine gun: Not used until the late 1800s, with the Maxim gun in 1884. Medieval armies had nothing that could shoot continuously.
Medieval weapons.Lightsaber: A fictional weapon from Star Wars, from 1977, and no match for a real longbow.
Medieval weapons.Taser: Developed in the 1970s and named after a boy's adventure novel, Tom Swift and His Electric Rifle. It is a modern device.
Medieval weapons.Torpedo: A self-propelled underwater missile, from the 1860s. The word first meant an electric ray fish.
Medieval weapons.Landmine: A buried explosive that needs gunpowder or modern explosives. Medieval armies had spiked caltrops instead.
Medieval weapons.Drone: A remotely piloted aircraft, practical in the late 20th century. Medieval sieges had none, though trained pigeons carried messages.
Medieval weapons.Water pistol: A toy, patented in the 1890s. Not a medieval weapon, though Greek fire siphons did spray liquid in battle.

Places the Vikings reached.Iceland: Settled by Norse from about 870. Its Althing, founded around 930, is one of the world's oldest parliaments.
Places the Vikings reached.Greenland: Erik the Red named it to lure settlers. Norse farms there survived for roughly 450 years before vanishing.
Places the Vikings reached.Newfoundland: At L'Anse aux Meadows the Norse left the only confirmed Viking site in North America, around the year 1000.
Places the Vikings reached.Ireland: Vikings founded Dublin, Waterford and Limerick as raiding bases, and Dublin's name comes from a Norse-era settlement.
Places the Vikings reached.England: The Danelaw covered much of eastern England, and Cnut ruled the whole kingdom from 1016.
Places the Vikings reached.Normandy: King Charles gave Rollo the land in 911. His Northmen became the Normans, who conquered England in 1066.
Places the Vikings reached.Kyiv: Norse traders called the Rus ruled it in the late 800s. Their name is the likely root of Russia.
Places the Vikings reached.Constantinople: Vikings served the Byzantine emperor as the Varangian Guard, and one left runic graffiti in the Hagia Sophia.
Places the Vikings reached.Scotland: Norse ruled Orkney, Shetland and the Hebrides. Shetland only passed from Norway to Scotland in 1469.
Places the Vikings reached.Faroe Islands: The name means sheep islands. Norse settlers arrived around the 800s, and Faroese still descends from Old Norse.
Places the Vikings reached.Paris: Vikings besieged it in 845 and again in 885 to 886. In 845 the king paid them thousands of pounds of silver to leave.
Places the Vikings reached.Seville: Vikings sailed up the river and sacked it in 844 before Moorish forces drove them off.
Places the Vikings reached.Australia: Europeans did not reach it until the 1600s, long after the Viking Age.
Places the Vikings reached.Japan: The Vikings never got there. Europeans arrived in Japan only in the 1500s.
Places the Vikings reached.Hawaii: Polynesians settled it long before Captain Cook arrived in 1778. No Vikings were ever there.
Places the Vikings reached.Brazil: Portuguese ships reached it in 1500. There is no evidence of Viking contact.
Places the Vikings reached.Mexico: No credible evidence of Viking contact. Their North American reach ended in the far northeast.
Places the Vikings reached.Peru: Home of the Inca, far beyond any Viking route. Spain arrived in the 1500s.
Places the Vikings reached.China: Vikings traded with Baghdad through Russian rivers, but Chinese records and finds show no Viking visit.
Places the Vikings reached.India: Their eastern trade routes ran to the Caspian and Baghdad, but not to India.
Places the Vikings reached.South Africa: Too far south; Bartolomeu Dias was the first European to round it, in 1488.
Places the Vikings reached.Madagascar: Settled by Austronesian sailors from Southeast Asia, and never visited by Vikings.
Places the Vikings reached.New Zealand: The Maori arrived around 1300 and Europeans only in the 1600s. No Viking connection.
Places the Vikings reached.Antarctica: First sighted in 1820, centuries after the Viking Age. It has no history of Norse visits.

Things from ancient China.Great Wall: Built by Emperor Qin Shi Huang and later extended by dynasties. Despite the legend, it can't be seen with the naked eye from space.
Things from ancient China.Terracotta Army: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers guard the first emperor's tomb, found in 1974 by farmers digging a well. Each face is unique.
Things from ancient China.Confucius: The sage whose sayings, collected as the Analects, shaped East Asian ethics and government for over two thousand years.
Things from ancient China.Silk Road: A network of trade routes linking China to the Mediterranean, named for the silk that flowed west. Ideas, religions and diseases traveled it too.
Things from ancient China.Qin Shi Huang: The first emperor of unified China, in 221 BC. He standardised writing, weights and axle widths across the realm.
Things from ancient China.Sun Tzu: The strategist credited with writing The Art of War around 2,500 years ago. His historical existence is still debated.
Things from ancient China.Lao Tzu: The legendary figure behind the Tao Te Ching, the foundation of Taoism. Tradition says he wrote it as he left China on an ox.
Things from ancient China.Oracle bones: Turtle shells and animal bones carved with questions for ancestors about 3,000 years ago. They hold the earliest known Chinese writing.
Things from ancient China.Han dynasty: The dynasty from 206 BC to AD 220, so influential that China's majority ethnic group still calls itself Han.
Things from ancient China.The Art of War: A military treatise of 13 chapters attributed to Sun Tzu. Modern business and sports figures still quote it.
Things from ancient China.Samurai: Trap: Japan's warrior class of the medieval era. Chinese and Japanese cultures differ, and the samurai belong to Japan.
Things from ancient China.Pharaoh: Trap: the ruler of ancient Egypt, a thousand miles from China. China's rulers were kings and later emperors.
Things from ancient China.Taj Mahal: Trap: the white marble tomb in Agra, built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in the 1600s. India, not China.
Things from ancient China.Angkor Wat: Trap: a vast 12th-century temple complex in Cambodia, built by the Khmer. It's Southeast Asian, not Chinese.
Things from ancient China.Shogun: Trap: Japan's hereditary military ruler. The shogunate lasted from 1192 to 1868, and it was Japanese through and through.
Things from ancient China.Ziggurat: Trap: stepped temple towers from Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq. They were built thousands of miles west of China.
Things from ancient China.Colosseum: Trap: Rome's amphitheatre, finished about AD 80. Rome and Han China traded silk but never really met.
Things from ancient China.Sphinx: Trap: the Great Sphinx at Giza in Egypt, carved from limestone with a lion's body, not a Chinese monument.
Things from ancient China.Haiku: Trap: a 17-syllable Japanese poem form. Though Chinese poetry influenced Japan, haiku is Japanese.
Things from ancient China.Machu Picchu: Trap: the 15th-century Inca citadel in Peru. Ancient China and the Andes never connected.
Things from ancient China.Gandhi: Trap: the leader of India's independence movement in the 1900s. Not ancient, and not Chinese.
Things from ancient China.Genghis Khan: Trap: a Mongol conqueror of the 1200s, medieval, not ancient. He attacked China, but wasn't Chinese.
Things from ancient China.Kabuki: Trap: Japanese theatre of the 1600s with elaborate makeup and male actors playing all roles. Japan, not China.
Things from ancient China.Kimono: Trap: Japan's traditional robe, tied with an obi sash. Its shape comes from Chinese dress, but it's Japanese.

Associated with the Inca Empire.Machu Picchu: The mountaintop citadel in Peru, built around 1450 for Emperor Pachacuti. The Spanish never found it, so it escaped destruction.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Cusco: The Inca capital in the Andes. Its name is said to mean 'navel' of the world, and its stonework still stands in the city's streets.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Quipu: A system of knotted cords used to record numbers and maybe stories. The Inca had no writing, yet governed millions with it.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Atahualpa: The last independent Sapa Inca, captured by Pizarro at Cajamarca in 1532. He filled a room with gold for ransom, then was executed anyway.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Pachacuti: The ninth Sapa Inca who turned a regional kingdom into an empire from about 1438. His name means 'earth-shaker'.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Inti: The Inca sun god. The emperors claimed to be his descendants, and gold was called 'sweat of the sun'.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Viracocha: The creator god in Andean belief, who made the sun, moon and humankind from Lake Titicaca's depths.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Sacsayhuaman: A fortress above Cusco with enormous stone blocks fitted without mortar, some weighing over a hundred tonnes.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Quechua: The language of the Inca, still spoken by millions in the Andes today. 'Llama' and 'puma' came into English from it.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Inca Trail: A trail of paved paths winding through the Andes to Machu Picchu, part of a road network of some 40,000 kilometres.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Coricancha: The Sun Temple of Cusco, whose walls were reportedly covered in gold. The Spanish built a church on its foundations.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Tenochtitlan: Trap: the Aztec capital, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, now Mexico City. The Aztecs were Mexican, not Andean.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Chichen Itza: Trap: a Maya city in the Yucatan with a famous stepped pyramid. Maya, not Inca, and a continent away.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Montezuma: Trap: Aztec emperor Moctezuma met Cortes in 1519. Mexican, not Andean, and he never met the Inca.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Quetzalcoatl: Trap: the feathered serpent god of Mesoamerica, linked to the Aztecs and Toltecs, not the Andes.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Teotihuacan: Trap: a vast ancient city near Mexico City with the Pyramid of the Sun. It predates the Aztecs, and has no Inca link.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Tikal: Trap: a great Maya city in Guatemala, with temples rising above the jungle canopy. Maya, not Inca.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Palenque: Trap: a Maya city in southern Mexico, known for the tomb of king Pakal. Different culture from the Inca.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Hernan Cortes: Trap: the Spanish conqueror of the Aztecs, in 1521. The Inca fell to a different conquistador, Francisco Pizarro.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Popol Vuh: Trap: the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala, telling their creation story, not an Inca work.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Cuauhtemoc: Trap: the last Aztec emperor, who resisted Cortes in 1521. He ruled in Mexico, not the Andes.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Templo Mayor: Trap: the main Aztec temple at the centre of Tenochtitlan, whose ruins lie beneath Mexico City.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Tlaloc: Trap: the Aztec rain and fertility god, worshipped in Tenochtitlan. He is Mexican, not Andean.
Associated with the Inca Empire.Huitzilopochtli: Trap: the Aztec god of war and the sun, to whom many sacrifices were made. Mexican, not an Inca deity.

Games played over 1000 years ago.Go: Invented in China over 2,500 years ago, it has more possible board positions than there are atoms in the observable universe.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Senet: Tutankhamun's tomb held senet sets, and Egyptians linked the game to the soul's journey through the afterlife.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Royal Game of Ur: Boards from about 2600 BC were found at Ur; the rules were decoded from a Babylonian clay tablet by Irving Finkel.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Chess: It descends from chaturanga, played in India around AD 600, whose pieces were chariots, elephants, cavalry and infantry.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Hnefatafl: A Viking strategy game of unequal sides: a king and his defenders against twice as many attackers.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Nine men's morris: Boards were scratched into Roman ruins and cathedral cloisters, and Shakespeare mentions it in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Knucklebones: Played with sheep ankle bones, it's an ancestor of both dice and the children's game jacks.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Mehen: An Egyptian board game shaped like a coiled snake, and its rules have been lost.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Latrunculi: A Roman strategy game of capturing soldiers; Latin authors praised it, but the exact rules are uncertain.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Monopoly: Lizzie Magie's 1904 Landlord's Game inspired it, and Parker Brothers sold it in 1935, so far from ancient.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Scrabble: Alfred Butts devised it in 1938 as Lexiko and later Criss-Crosswords, so only around ninety years old.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Risk: French filmmaker Albert Lamorisse designed it in 1957 as La Conquête du Monde.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Clue: Anthony Pratt invented it in the 1940s while stuck in air-raid shelters; Britain calls it Cluedo.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Battleship: It grew from a pencil-and-paper game and became a plastic board game in 1967.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Connect Four: It came out in 1974, centuries after the old games.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Trivial Pursuit: Two Canadian journalists made it in 1979 after finding the Scrabble set missing pieces.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Candy Land: Eleanor Abbott made it in 1948 while recovering from polio, for children in a hospital ward.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Othello: Othello is from 1970s Japan, though it's based on the 1880s English game Reversi.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Stratego: A Dutch game of 1946 based on French L'Attaque, which Napoleonic soldiers would not have known.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Mahjong: Mahjong is from 19th-century China, nowhere near a thousand years old.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Poker: It took shape in early 1800s New Orleans, perhaps from the French game poque.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Bingo: It traces to a 1500s Italian lottery, but the modern game and the name bingo come from the 1930s.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Twister: Launched in 1966, it became a hit after Johnny Carson played it with Eva Gabor on TV.
Games played over 1000 years ago.Catan: Klaus Teuber, a German dental technician, published it in 1995 as The Settlers of Catan.

Things that strain or drain liquid.Colander: Colanders are named from the Latin for 'to strain,' and the sieve shape pastas drain in has been used for centuries.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Sieve: A sieve separates fine from coarse; the phrase 'memory like a sieve' means it lets everything slip through.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Tea strainer: Tea strainers catch loose leaves, and the tea bag itself was reportedly invented by accident around 1908 by a New York merchant.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Salad spinner: A salad spinner uses centrifugal force to fling water off greens, so it works just like a washing machine's spin cycle.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Slotted spoon: A slotted spoon lets liquid fall through the openings so you can lift out poached eggs or boiled vegetables without the water.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Cheesecloth: Cheesecloth is a loosely woven cotton that's used to strain cheese curds, and it comes in grades by thread count.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Coffee filter: Melitta Bentz invented the paper coffee filter in 1908 in Germany, using blotting paper from her son's school notebook.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Spider strainer: The spider strainer is a wide wire-mesh basket on a long bamboo handle, and it's named for its web-like look.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Sink strainer: A sink strainer stops food scraps from clogging pipes, and plumbers say food in drains is a main cause of blockages.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Ladle: A ladle scoops liquid, and it holds the soup rather than letting it pass through; some are marked in ounces.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Whisk: The whisk adds air to eggs or cream, and the balloon shape of the wires helps trap it as you beat.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Mixing bowl: A mixing bowl holds liquid in rather than draining it, and they're often made of stainless steel, glass, or ceramic.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Funnel: A funnel guides liquid into a narrow opening, which is different from straining, though some have built-in filters.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Measuring cup: A measuring cup tells you how much, and a US cup is about 240 milliliters, so it measures but never strains.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Tongs: Tongs grip food rather than separate liquid, and the design dates back to ancient blacksmiths pulling hot metal.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Spatula: A spatula's name goes back to a Latin word for a flat piece of wood, and it flips rather than drains.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough, and the French style tapered pin has no handles so a baker can feel the dough better.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Pitcher: A pitcher holds and pours liquids, but it doesn't strain them, unless it has a filter, like those in water-purifier jugs.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Cutting board: A cutting board does absorb a bit of juice, but its grooves just catch liquid, not drain it away.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Saucepan: A saucepan cooks liquids rather than straining them, and it's the usual partner of a colander when you boil pasta.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Grater: A grater shreds food into bits, and its most famous use is for hard cheeses like Parmesan.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Turkey baster: A baster sucks up juices to pour back on a roast; it moves liquid but doesn't strain it, so it's a trap.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Gravy boat: A gravy boat holds and pours the sauce, and some have a spout below the surface so fat floats on top.
Things that strain or drain liquid.Pastry brush: A pastry brush spreads butter or egg wash, and it holds liquid among its bristles, not letting it strain through.

Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Nails: Nails come in sizes called pennies, written as 'd', which once reflected the price per hundred.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Screws: Screws grip far better than nails, and a Phillips head was designed to let a driver slip out before over-tightening.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Paint: Paint stores offer color matching by machine, so a tiny sample can be reproduced in any shade.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Hammer: The claw hammer's split end can pull nails, and it has changed little in design for centuries.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Light bulbs: Light bulbs have shifted to LEDs, which last about 25 times longer than old incandescent ones.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Duct tape: Duct tape was invented in the Second World War to seal ammunition cases, and it was first called duck tape.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Sandpaper: Sandpaper's grit number tells you how coarse it is, where a lower number means rougher.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Hinges: Hinges are one of the oldest bits of hardware, with versions found in ancient Egypt.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Extension cord: An extension cord must be rated for the load it carries or its wires can overheat.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Padlock: Padlocks with a keyed cylinder have a design that goes back to ancient Rome.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Drill bits: Drill bits are matched to the material, with different shapes for wood, metal and masonry.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Caulk: Caulk seals gaps around tubs and windows, and it's usually silicone or acrylic latex.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Lettuce: Lettuce is sold in grocery stores, and no hardware shop stocks it.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Birthday cake: A birthday cake is for a bakery and has no place among drills and nails.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Prescription drugs: Prescription drugs need a pharmacist and a license, which a hardware store doesn't have.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Fresh fish: Fresh fish belongs at a fishmonger or market, not at the hardware shop.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Movie tickets: Movie tickets are sold at a cinema, so no, not at the hardware store.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Haircut: A haircut is a service you'd get from a barber, and tools can't help.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Wedding dress: A wedding dress comes from a bridal boutique, quite far from the paint aisle.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Sushi: Sushi is sold at a restaurant or market, though not near the hammers.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Puppy: A puppy is a living creature that you'd get from a shelter or breeder.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Concert tickets: Concert tickets are sold online or at a venue, not at the hardware store.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Live lobster: Live lobster is sold at a seafood market, and it's rarely found with the tools.
Things you'd buy at a hardware store.Croissants: Croissants are baked goods from a bakery, and the hardware store doesn't sell them.

Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. House: Gregory House is a Sherlock Holmes homage: he lives at 221B, has a friend named Wilson, and is addicted to Vicodin.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Watson: John Watson, the loyal friend of Sherlock Holmes, was an army doctor, and Arthur Conan Doyle himself was a physician.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Jekyll: Dr. Jekyll is the doctor in Stevenson's 1886 novella who turns into Mr. Hyde, and his name inspired the phrase Jekyll and Hyde.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Dolittle: Hugh Lofting's Dr. Dolittle is a physician who becomes a vet and learns to talk to animals, from stories written in trenches.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Strange: Stephen Strange is a surgeon turned sorcerer; before he gained magic, he was a gifted neurosurgeon.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. McCoy: Leonard McCoy of Star Trek, nicknamed Bones, is a ship's doctor, famous for the line I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Zhivago: Yuri Zhivago is a doctor and poet in Boris Pasternak's novel, and the book was banned in the USSR.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Quinn: Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman followed Michaela Quinn, a Boston doctor who moves to Colorado in the 1860s.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Hibbert: Julius Hibbert of The Simpsons is Springfield's cheerful, laughing doctor, whose chuckle is his trademark.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Doc Martin: Doc Martin is a grumpy surgeon with a blood phobia, who relocates to Cornwall in the British series set in Port Isaac.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Who: The Doctor of Doctor Who is not a medical doctor at all, and the character's true name is a great mystery.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Seuss: Theodor Geisel took the title Dr. as a joke, and he never earned a medical degree; his honorary ones came later.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Dre: Dr. Dre's nickname came from basketball star Julius Erving, Dr. J, and he is a rapper and producer, not a doctor.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Pepper: Dr. Pepper is a soft drink from Waco, Texas, created in 1885, and there is no actual doctor in it.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Octopus: Otto Octavius, a Spider-Man foe, has a doctorate in nuclear physics, not medicine, and his eight limbs are mechanical arms.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. No: Dr. No from the first Bond film is a villain with metal hands, and his doctorate is in philosophy, not medicine.
