Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Doom: Victor von Doom of Marvel is a scientist and sorcerer, and a monarch of Latveria, but no medical doctor.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Robotnik: Dr. Robotnik, the Sonic the Hedgehog villain, has an IQ of 300 but holds a doctorate in robotics, not medicine.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Facilier: Facilier, from Disney's The Princess and the Frog, is the Shadow Man and a voodoo villain, not a physician.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Horrible: Dr. Horrible's Sing-Along Blog was a 2008 web musical by Joss Whedon, and the villain has a doctorate in evil.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Claw: Dr. Claw, the faceless foe of Inspector Gadget, is a criminal mastermind, and his face is never seen on screen.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Hook: Dr. Hook and the Medicine Show was a 1970s band known for songs like Sylvia's Mother, with no actual doctor involved.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. J: Dr. J is the nickname of basketball legend Julius Erving, who dunked from the free throw line and was not a physician.
Fictional characters who are medical doc.Dr. Martens: Dr. Martens boots were designed in the 1940s by German doctor Klaus Maertens, but they are a footwear brand, not a character.

Organs in your abdomen.Stomach: The stomach's lining replaces itself every few days, which protects it from its own strong acid.
Organs in your abdomen.Liver: The liver can regrow after partial removal, the only internal organ that does so so well.
Organs in your abdomen.Spleen: The spleen filters old red blood cells, and people can live without it, with a higher infection risk.
Organs in your abdomen.Pancreas: The pancreas does two jobs, making digestive enzymes and the hormone insulin.
Organs in your abdomen.Gallbladder: The gallbladder stores bile, and many people live perfectly well after having it removed.
Organs in your abdomen.Kidney: Each kidney holds about a million filtering units, and people can live healthily with just one.
Organs in your abdomen.Small intestine: The small intestine is the longest part of the gut, several meters of tube where most nutrients are absorbed.
Organs in your abdomen.Large intestine: The large intestine is shorter but wider than the small one, hence its name, and it reabsorbs water.
Organs in your abdomen.Appendix: The appendix sits in the lower right of the abdomen and may shelter helpful gut bacteria.
Organs in your abdomen.Heart: The heart sits in the chest, shielded by the ribcage, above the diaphragm.
Organs in your abdomen.Lung: Lungs are in the chest, separated from the abdomen by the diaphragm.
Organs in your abdomen.Brain: The brain sits in the skull, though the gut has its own 'second brain' of neurons.
Organs in your abdomen.Thyroid: The butterfly-shaped thyroid sits in the neck.
Organs in your abdomen.Trachea: The trachea, or windpipe, runs through the neck into the chest.
Organs in your abdomen.Thymus: The thymus sits behind the breastbone and shrinks after puberty.
Organs in your abdomen.Larynx: The larynx sits in the neck and houses the vocal cords.
Organs in your abdomen.Tonsil: Tonsils are patches of immune tissue at the back of the throat.
Organs in your abdomen.Pituitary gland: The pea-sized pituitary gland sits at the base of the brain and directs other glands.
Organs in your abdomen.Eyeball: The eyeball sits in a skull socket, nowhere near the belly.
Organs in your abdomen.Tongue: A tongue is made of muscle and sits in the mouth, well away from the abdomen.
Organs in your abdomen.Cochlea: The snail-shaped cochlea in the inner ear turns sound vibrations into nerve signals.
Organs in your abdomen.Sinus: Sinuses are air spaces in the skull bones around the nose.
Organs in your abdomen.Vocal cords: Vocal cords are folds of tissue in the larynx, in the neck.
Organs in your abdomen.Adam's apple: The Adam's apple is the larynx bulge in the neck, more visible in many men.

Things you do with your eyes.Blink: People blink around 15 to 20 times a minute, but far less while staring at a screen.
Things you do with your eyes.Wink: A wink needs just one eyelid, and because it's deliberate it often signals flirting or a shared joke.
Things you do with your eyes.Squint: Squinting sharpens vision by narrowing the opening and cutting scattered light, like a natural pinhole camera.
Things you do with your eyes.Stare: Staring is considered rude in many cultures, and among apes a direct, steady stare can be a threat signal.
Things you do with your eyes.Glance: A glance is a very quick look, and your eyes make about three tiny jumps a second, called saccades.
Things you do with your eyes.Gaze: Gaze is longer and softer than a glance, and a Japanese study found mutual gazing raises oxytocin in dogs and owners.
Things you do with your eyes.Peek: Babies around one love peekaboo because they're still learning that hidden things keep existing.
Things you do with your eyes.Glare: A glare is an angry stare, and in many animals direct eye contact is a threat rather than a friendly sign.
Things you do with your eyes.Cry: Humans may be the only animals that cry tears of emotion, which come from the lacrimal glands above the eyes.
Things you do with your eyes.Peer: To peer is to look hard at something hard to see, often paired with squinting, as in peering through fog.
Things you do with your eyes.Gawk: Gawk probably comes from an old dialect word gowk, meaning a cuckoo or fool, so gawking was originally foolish staring.
Things you do with your eyes.Eye-roll: An eye-roll is a silent way to show contempt, moving the eyes upward, often along with a head tilt.
Things you do with your eyes.Sniff: Dogs sniff in short bursts that let them keep catching odors even as they breathe out, but it's a nose job, not an eye one.
Things you do with your eyes.Chew: Chewing is jaw work, and thorough chewing helps digestion by breaking food into smaller pieces.
Things you do with your eyes.Whistle: Whistling uses lips and breath, and in the Turkish village of Kuskoy people talk across valleys with a whistled language.
Things you do with your eyes.Clap: Concert audiences often fall into rhythmic, synchronized clapping, which is hands work, not eyes.
Things you do with your eyes.Shrug: A shrug raises the shoulders, and it's one of the few gestures understood almost everywhere.
Things you do with your eyes.Nod: Nodding moves the neck, and the phrase nod off comes from heads drooping when we get sleepy.
Things you do with your eyes.Hum: Humming is done with a closed mouth and vocal cords, and it's often linked with feeling relaxed.
Things you do with your eyes.Snore: Snoring comes from vibrating throat tissue, and it happens while the eyes are tightly shut in sleep.
Things you do with your eyes.Lick: A cat's tongue is covered in tiny hooked barbs that work like a comb, which is why licking feels rough.
Things you do with your eyes.Sip: Sipping uses lips and cheeks to draw liquid slowly, and the eyes have nothing to do with it.
Things you do with your eyes.Gargle: Saltwater gargles are a long-standing home remedy for sore throats, and they're a mouth-and-throat activity, not an eye one.
Things you do with your eyes.Tap: Tapping fingers or toes is a hand or foot habit, and a fast-tapping one often signals impatience.

Things a classic circus clown wears.Red nose: Clowns often call it the world's smallest mask, and putting it on is said to switch a performer into character instantly.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Oversized shoes: Long floppy shoes make every step comically awkward, letting clowns trip and stagger in ways that look dangerous but are carefully rehearsed.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Rainbow wig: Wild wigs keep a clown readable from the far seats of a big top, where tiny facial expressions would be lost.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Face paint: Each clown traditionally owns a unique face design, and a clown egg register even keeps painted eggs to record them like trademarks.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Baggy trousers: Huge pants leave room to hide props, and their sagging shape is part of the physical comedy of tripping and tumbling.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Giant bow tie: A bow tie scaled up to absurd size is a clown staple; some spin or squirt water, turning formalwear into a gag.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Squirting flower: A lapel flower that sprays water is one of the oldest clown gags, turning a polite sniff into a soaking.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Polka dot suit: Loud patterns like polka dots help a clown pop against the crowd and stage lights, unlike the plain suit of the ringmaster.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Ruffled collar: The big frilled collar descends from Pierrot and other commedia dell'arte costumes, which helped shape the clown look.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Hard hat: A hard hat is workwear for builders; on a clown it only appears as a joke, which is why it isn't part of the classic outfit.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Scrubs: Hospital clown programmes do exist, but those performers still wear clown outfits rather than medical scrubs.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Wetsuit: A wetsuit traps a thin layer of water warmed by the body, which suits divers and surfers but not a circus ring.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Hi-vis vest: Hi-vis vests make workers noticeable to drivers, but clowns already rely on bright colours instead of reflective strips.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Spacesuit: Spacesuits are built to hold air pressure and block radiation in orbit, which is a long way from the circus ring.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Ski goggles: Ski goggles cut glare off snow at speed; a clown's painted face is meant to be seen, so goggles would hide the show.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Chain mail: Chain mail is knight armour made of thousands of linked metal rings, and it would be far too heavy for a pratfall act.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Lab coat: White lab coats shield scientists from spills, whereas a clown would rather wear something to ruin with a custard pie.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Riding boots: Riding boots belong to horse riders, and circus riders do wear them, but clowns stick to comically oversized shoes.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Bearskin hat: The tall fur bearskin is ceremonial headgear of the British Foot Guards, famous for standing rigid and never smiling.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Kevlar helmet: Kevlar is a strong synthetic fibre used in bulletproof gear and combat helmets, serious kit far from a clown's costume.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Judge's robe: Judges wear robes to signal impartial authority; a clown in one would be a courtroom gag, not the classic outfit.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Diving helmet: Classic brass diving helmets are heavy, pressurised gear for underwater work, so no clown outfit includes one.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Welding mask: A welding mask has a dark filter to shield eyes from an intense arc, and it would hide the face paint a clown relies on.
Things a classic circus clown wears.Toga: The toga was the draped wool garment of Roman citizens; it needs careful arranging, unlike a clown's baggy costume.

Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Puck: Also called Robin Goodfellow, he mistakenly puts the love potion on the wrong Athenian's eyes and sets the chaos off.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Oberon: The fairy king quarrels with his queen over a changeling boy, and plots to humiliate her with a love potion.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Titania: The fairy queen is made to fall in love with a man wearing a donkey's head, a spell Oberon cast as revenge.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Bottom: The weaver gets a donkey's head from Puck and plays Pyramus in the amateur actors' play-within-a-play.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Lysander: A young Athenian who loves Hermia, but who is bewitched by Puck's potion into chasing Helena.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Demetrius: He chases Hermia, whom her father wants him to marry, until the love potion makes him adore Helena.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Hermia: She defies her father's wish for her to marry Demetrius and flees to the woods with Lysander.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Helena: She chases Demetrius through the forest in the beginning, though he scorns her, and then is adored by both men.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Theseus: The Duke of Athens, whose wedding to Hippolyta frames the entire story, and who later sits as audience for the play-within-a-play.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Hippolyta: The Queen of the Amazons is about to marry Theseus; in Greek myth he defeated her people.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Peter Quince: The carpenter who directs the troupe of amateur actors, whose rehearsals in the woods provide the play's comic relief.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Egeus: Hermia's father demands that she marry Demetrius, invoking an Athenian law that could condemn her to death.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Flute: The bellows-mender is cast as the female lead Thisbe in the actors' play, and is embarrassed to be playing a woman.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Snout: The tinker plays Wall in the actors' play, reciting his lines while holding up his fingers as a chink.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Ariel: The airy spirit serving Prospero belongs to The Tempest, not to the woods near Athens.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Caliban: The island creature whom Prospero enslaved belongs to The Tempest, not this play.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Prospero: The exiled magician duke of The Tempest, so not in this comedy of fairies.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Miranda: Prospero's daughter, from The Tempest, has no place among these Athenians.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Viola: The shipwrecked heroine of Twelfth Night disguises herself as a boy, so she is from a different comedy.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Feste: The jester in Twelfth Night who sings the songs there, so from another comedy.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Sebastian: Viola's twin brother in Twelfth Night, and also a name in The Tempest, but not in this play.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Rosalind: The heroine of As You Like It disguises herself as a boy in the Forest of Arden.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Touchstone: The jester in As You Like It who follows the exiled court to Arden.
Characters in A Midsummer Night's Dream.Falstaff: The comic knight of the Henry plays and The Merry Wives of Windsor, not part of the Athenian forest.

Places at Hogwarts.Great Hall: The Great Hall's ceiling is enchanted to mirror the sky above, and it seats four long house tables.
Places at Hogwarts.Whomping Willow: The Whomping Willow was planted the year Lupin arrived to guard the secret passage to the Shrieking Shack.
Places at Hogwarts.Room of Requirement: The Room of Requirement appears only when someone needs it, and it becomes whatever they need, from a training room to storage.
Places at Hogwarts.Quidditch pitch: The Quidditch pitch has three goal hoops at each end and stands for the sport played on broomsticks.
Places at Hogwarts.Chamber of Secrets: The Chamber of Secrets is Salazar Slytherin's hidden chamber, guarded by a basilisk, and entered through a bathroom sink.
Places at Hogwarts.Owlery: The Owlery is a tower where hundreds of school owls roost, and students send letters from it.
Places at Hogwarts.Forbidden Forest: The Forbidden Forest holds centaurs, unicorns, and Aragog's giant spiders, and students are not allowed in.
Places at Hogwarts.Hospital wing: In the Hospital Wing, Madam Pomfrey can mend broken bones overnight, though regrowing them with Skele-Gro hurts.
Places at Hogwarts.Restricted Section: The Restricted Section of the library holds dark books and requires a teacher's signature.
Places at Hogwarts.Hagrid's hut: Hagrid's hut sits at the edge of the Forbidden Forest, with a pumpkin patch and his dog Fang.
Places at Hogwarts.Gryffindor Tower: Gryffindor Tower is reached through the Fat Lady's portrait, who demands a password.
Places at Hogwarts.Astronomy Tower: The Astronomy Tower is the highest in the castle, where Dumbledore dies, and where classes track the stars.
Places at Hogwarts.Moving staircases: The castle has 142 staircases, and some change direction, while one leads somewhere different on Fridays.
Places at Hogwarts.Diagon Alley: Diagon Alley is hidden in London behind the Leaky Cauldron, where Harry buys his wand at Ollivanders.
Places at Hogwarts.Gringotts: Gringotts is the goblin-run wizarding bank in London, with vaults deep underground and a guard dragon.
Places at Hogwarts.Leaky Cauldron: The Leaky Cauldron is a London pub whose back wall opens into Diagon Alley, and Muggles cannot see it.
Places at Hogwarts.Ministry of Magic: The Ministry of Magic is underground in London, reached by a red telephone box, not at Hogwarts.
Places at Hogwarts.Azkaban: Azkaban is the wizard prison on a North Sea island, guarded by Dementors until they were removed.
Places at Hogwarts.Platform 9 3/4: Platform 9 3/4 is at King's Cross, reached by walking through the barrier between platforms nine and ten.
Places at Hogwarts.The Burrow: The Burrow is the Weasleys' lopsided home in Ottery St Catchpole, held up, they joke, only by magic.
Places at Hogwarts.Privet Drive: Privet Drive, number four, is where Harry grew up with the Dursleys, sleeping in a cupboard under the stairs.
Places at Hogwarts.Hogsmeade: Hogsmeade is the only entirely wizard village in Britain, with Honeydukes and the Three Broomsticks, but it's off the school grounds.
Places at Hogwarts.Knockturn Alley: Knockturn Alley is a dark-magic street off Diagon Alley, where Harry ends up lost after a Floo powder slip.
Places at Hogwarts.St Mungo's: St Mungo's is the Hospital for Magical Maladies and Injuries in London, where Neville's parents are patients.

Things that don't belong in a microwave.Aluminum foil: Metal in a microwave can spark because electric charge builds at sharp edges and crumples, so crinkled foil is especially risky.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Metal fork: Forks have tines close together that concentrate charge, so they can arc and spark; the sparks can even damage the oven.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Whole egg in shell: Steam builds inside the sealed shell faster than it can escape, so an egg can burst, sometimes even after leaving the oven.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Stainless steel mug: Steel reflects microwaves instead of letting them through, so food inside heats poorly and the oven can be damaged.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Grapes: Cut a grape almost in half, microwave it, and the two halves form a glowing plasma spark, a favorite physics demo.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Gold-rimmed plate: A thin metal trim on a plate can spark and arc in the microwave, burning the decoration and sometimes cracking the plate.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Twist tie: The thin wire inside twist ties can spark in a microwave, and sometimes starts a small fire in a bag.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Chinese takeout pail: Those folded takeout pails often have a thin metal wire handle, which can spark, so transfer the food to a plate first.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Cast iron pan: Cast iron blocks microwaves, so food doesn't heat properly and a heavy pan could damage the oven.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Metal mixing bowl: Metal reflects microwaves instead of letting them cook the food, and the reflected energy can harm the magnetron.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Ceramic plate: A plain ceramic plate usually works fine, as microwaves pass through it, though glaze with metallic paint is a trap.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Paper towel: Plain paper towels are fine for covering food in short bursts; they're basically transparent to microwaves.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Popcorn bag: Microwave popcorn bags have a susceptor lining that absorbs microwaves, which helps kernels reach popping temperature.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Mug of water: Water heated in a smooth mug can superheat past boiling without bubbling, then erupt when you disturb it, so be careful.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Leftover pasta: Microwaves heat water molecules, so a splash of water on leftover pasta stops it from drying out when reheated.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Butter: Butter melts easily in the microwave, but covering it prevents splatter, since fat can heat suddenly and spit.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Wax paper: Wax paper is safe to use as a loose cover in the microwave, unlike foil, because it contains no metal.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Oatmeal: Microwaving oatmeal is a popular shortcut, but a larger bowl helps since it foams up and tends to boil over.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Pyrex dish: Microwave-friendly glass is a good heat-proof choice, though sudden temperature changes can shock it and crack it.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Frozen peas: Frozen peas are fine in the microwave and heat quickly, since they're small and mostly water.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Soup: Soup is a microwave staple because it's mostly water, but stirring halfway through avoids hot and cold spots.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Cooked rice: Reheating rice in the microwave is fine if it was cooled quickly, as leftover rice can harbor bacteria that survive reheating.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Baked beans: Baked beans heat well in the microwave if covered, as the thick sauce can burst and splatter if left open.
Things that don't belong in a microwave.Corn on the cob: You can microwave corn in its husk, which steams it neatly, as the husk traps moisture and cooks evenly.

Inside a car's passenger cabin.Steering wheel: The wheel in your hands has often been replaced by a joystick in concept cars, though the round one has dominated since the early 1900s.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Glovebox: Despite the name, glovebox was a place for driving gloves in early open cars, when drivers needed them against the cold.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Rearview mirror: The first rearview mirror is credited to Ray Harroun's 1911 Indianapolis 500 winner, who used it to drive without a riding mechanic.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Seatbelt: Volvo engineer Nils Bohlin invented the modern three-point belt in 1959, and Volvo gave away the patent to save lives.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Gearstick: In British English a gearstick, in American a shifter; a growing share of new cars now have just a dial or buttons instead.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Cup holder: Cup holders became standard in the US only from around the 1980s and 90s, when fast food made drinking in cars normal.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Dashboard: The word dashboard first meant a board on a horse-drawn carriage to stop mud being "dashed" up at the driver.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Handbrake: The handbrake usually works on the rear wheels through a cable, which is why it still works if the main brakes fail.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Sun visor: Many sun visors carry a small vanity mirror, and some carry a tiny strip with the car's warning labels.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Headrest: Headrests are mainly a safety device against whiplash in rear-end collisions, which is why they're set at about ear level.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Airbag: An airbag inflates in about 20 to 40 milliseconds, faster than a blink, by a chemical reaction that produces nitrogen gas.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Horn: Car horns in the US are often tuned to sound a pair of notes, and the standard dual-tone setup tends to sound a chord.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Speedometer: The speedometer was patented in the 1900s by Croatian inventor Josip Belušić, who called his version a velocimeter.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Spark plug: The spark plug ignites the fuel inside the engine's cylinder, so it lives under the bonnet, not in the cabin.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Radiator: The radiator cools the engine under the bonnet; the cabin heater is a smaller cousin that uses the same hot coolant.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Alternator: The alternator charges the battery while the engine runs; it's mounted on the engine, not inside the cabin.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Dipstick: A dipstick checks engine oil under the bonnet; it's a thin metal rod that shows how much oil is left.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Muffler: The muffler (silencer in Britain) sits under the car; its chambers cancel out sound waves to cut engine noise.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Exhaust pipe: The exhaust pipe carries burned gases away at the rear, and its fumes are why it sits outside the cabin.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Mudflap: Mudflaps hang behind wheels to catch spray and stones; they're outside the car, with the wheels.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Hubcap: A hubcap covers the wheel's centre to keep out dirt; it's on the outside of the car, and thieves often snatch them.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.License plate: License plates are required on the exterior front and back, though in some US states only a rear plate is needed.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Fan belt: The fan belt drives the cooling fan and other parts from the engine; it's under the bonnet, not in the cabin.
Inside a car's passenger cabin.Brake disc: The brake disc sits behind each wheel and can glow red hot under heavy braking, as in motor racing.

Traditional Japanese clothing.Kimono: Kimono means 'thing to wear'. One takes about 12 meters of fabric, and the left side goes over the right for the living; reversed is for the dead.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Yukata: A light cotton kimono worn in summer, often to festivals and hot-spring inns. Unlike silk kimonos, it can be washed at home.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Obi: The wide sash around a kimono. Some obi are 4 meters long and tied in elaborate knots that differ by occasion and age.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Hakama: Pleated, wide-legged trousers worn over a kimono. Samurai wore them originally, and they are still worn in martial arts like aikido and kendo.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Geta: Wooden sandals raised on two blocks, to keep feet above muddy or wet streets. The clacking sound is part of their charm.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Tabi: Split-toe socks designed so that the big toe sits separately, letting wearers use thong sandals like geta or zori.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Haori: A short jacket worn over a kimono. Once reserved for men, it became popular among women in the Edo period.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Zori: Flat sandals with a thong strap, traditionally made of straw. Formal ones are lacquered or fabric-covered.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Happi coat: A loose straight-sleeved jacket worn at festivals and by shop workers, often printed with a crest or shop name.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Hanbok: Hanbok is traditional Korean clothing, known for bright colors and a high-waisted, flowing silhouette. It's not Japanese.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Qipao: The qipao, or cheongsam, is a fitted Chinese dress with a high collar. It rose to popularity in 1920s Shanghai.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Sari: A sari is a single length of fabric, up to six meters, draped around the body in India and South Asia.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Ao dai: The Vietnamese ao dai is a long fitted tunic worn over trousers. It is a national symbol of Vietnam.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Dirndl: A dirndl is a Bavarian and Austrian dress. The side the bow is tied on can signal a woman's relationship status.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Kilt: The kilt is Scottish, with tartan patterns tied to clans. It is also traditional Scottish dress, not Japanese.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Poncho: A poncho is a cloak with a head hole, native to Andean South America, used for centuries to guard against cold.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Sarong: A wrap-around cloth from Southeast Asia and the Pacific, worn by men and women. Not Japanese.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Kaftan: The kaftan is a long loose robe from Persia and the Ottoman world, so it belongs elsewhere than Japan.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Dashiki: Dashiki is a colorful West African garment, the name comes from the Yoruba word dàńṣíkí. It became popular in the US in the 1960s.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Lederhosen: Leather shorts from Bavaria and Austria, originally working clothes. The name means 'leather trousers' in German.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Sombrero: The sombrero is Mexican, a wide-brimmed hat whose name comes from the Spanish word 'sombra', meaning shade.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Fez: A felt cap with a tassel, named after the Moroccan city of Fez. It became Ottoman headwear before being banned in Turkey in 1925.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Beret: A soft, round cap associated with France and Basque regions. Many armies and the French Resistance wore it.
Traditional Japanese clothing.Tunic: A tunic is a loose, simple garment worn since Roman and Greek times. It is not specifically Japanese.

Words that can come before \"coat\".Rain: Charles Macintosh patented waterproof fabric in 1823, and raincoats are still called macs.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Over: Also the term for a layer of paint or varnish applied on top.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Trench: Developed for officers in World War I, with epaulets and belt loops; Burberry and Aquascutum made them.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Pea: A thick wool jacket, favored by sailors; the name likely comes from Dutch pij, coarse cloth.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Waist: A vest in British English, called a vest in American, worn under a jacket.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Top: Topcoat is also the final layer on nail polish or paint.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Petti: Petticoat comes from petty coat, a small coat, worn beneath a skirt.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Tail: Gave rise to the idiom riding on someone's coattails, from the long back flaps.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Turn: A turncoat switches sides, an idea from turning a coat inside out to show a different color.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Under: Also an animal's soft, dense underfur, which keeps it warm beneath the outer layer.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Sugar: Also literal: candy shells such as Jordan almonds are a hard layer of sugar.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Lab: The white coat caught on in the late 1800s as medicine tried to look scientific.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Fur: A British idiom, all fur coat and no knickers, mocks someone who is all show.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Hat: Hats and coats go together, but hatcoat isn't a word.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Shoe: Shoecoat is not a word; shoes get horns, laces and trees instead.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Sock: Sock comes from Latin soccus, a light slipper, but sockcoat isn't a word.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Sleeve: A sleeveless coat is a vest or gilet, so sleevecoat does not exist.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Skirt: Skirt comes before coat in no word; petticoat is the closest.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Sandal: Sandal comes from Greek sandalon; sandalcoat is not a word.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Boot: In British English, boot also means a car's trunk, but bootcoat isn't a word.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Glove: Latex gloves were invented in 1889 for a nurse whose hands were irritated by chemicals; but glovecoat isn't a word.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Belt: Trench coats have belts, yet beltcoat isn't a word.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Tie: Neckties come from the cravats of Croatian soldiers in 17th-century France; tiecoat is not a word.
Words that can come before \"coat\".Wind: Windcoat isn't a standard word; windbreaker and windcheater are the usual terms.

Classic playground games.Hopscotch: Hopscotch dates back to ancient Rome, where soldiers reportedly ran drills in hopscotch-like courts to build footwork.
Classic playground games.Tag: Tag is among the oldest games, found across cultures. It is basically a rehearsal of chase and escape and builds real fitness.
Classic playground games.Hide and seek: Hide and seek is played worldwide under many names; in some countries kids call 'ready or not' before they search.
Classic playground games.Red rover: Red Rover has two teams calling a player to run and break their linked arms. It's now banned in some schools for injuries.
Classic playground games.Kick the can: Kick the can mixes hide and seek with tag: a seeker has to guard a can that hiders try to kick to free the captured.
Classic playground games.Jump rope: Jump rope has roots in ancient Egypt and China, and rhymes chanted during it often passed down through generations.
Classic playground games.Capture the flag: Capture the flag is a team game of stealing the other side's flag while avoiding being tagged; it is also played by the military in training.
Classic playground games.Freeze tag: Freeze tag has tagged players stand still until a teammate unfreezes them, giving tag a team-saving twist.
Classic playground games.Four square: Four square uses a court of four boxes and a rubber ball; it grew popular on American blacktop and is now played in leagues.
Classic playground games.Duck duck goose: In duck duck goose, the child tapping heads says 'duck' until picking someone as 'goose'. In Minnesota it's called 'duck, duck, gray duck'.
Classic playground games.Hula hoop: The hula hoop became a craze in 1958, when Wham-O sold some 25 million in its first months.
Classic playground games.Stickball: Stickball is a street version of baseball, using a broomstick and a rubber ball, popular in New York City.
Classic playground games.Simon says: Simon Says teaches careful listening: you obey orders only if they begin with the phrase. The game is centuries old.
Classic playground games.Chess: Chess is a board game, not a playground game, with roots in sixth-century India.
Classic playground games.Scrabble: Scrabble was invented in 1938 by Alfred Butts, who counted letter frequencies in the New York Times to set tile values.
Classic playground games.Monopoly: Monopoly was based on The Landlord's Game, created by Elizabeth Magie to show how land ownership enriches landlords.
Classic playground games.Solitaire: Solitaire is a one-player card game, so it can't be a playground classic; it is Europe's patience tradition.
Classic playground games.Sudoku: Sudoku, despite its Japanese name, came from American puzzle Number Place, and became popular after Japan's puzzle company Nikoli renamed it.
Classic playground games.Jigsaw puzzle: A jigsaw puzzle was originally a hand-cut map used for teaching geography, invented in the 1760s.
Classic playground games.Crossword: The first crossword appeared in the New York World in 1913, created by Arthur Wynne as a diamond-shaped 'word-cross'.
Classic playground games.Go Fish: Go Fish is a card game for families, not outdoors, played by asking for matching ranks.
Classic playground games.Battleship: Battleship started as a pencil-and-paper game played by soldiers before Milton Bradley made the plastic version.
Classic playground games.Tetris: Tetris was made in 1984 by Soviet programmer Alexey Pajitnov; it's the best-known video game puzzle.
Classic playground games.Mahjong: Mahjong is a tile game from China played by four players, with a clack of tiles; it isn't a playground game.

Gods and spirits of love and desire.Eros: In the oldest Greek myths a primal force of creation, later shown as Aphrodite's winged son with a bow.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Aphrodite: Said by Greek myth to have been born from sea foam near Cyprus, which gave her the title 'foam-born'.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Venus: The Roman counterpart of Aphrodite; the planet shining brightest in the evening sky is named for her.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Cupid: The Roman Eros, whose chubby baby look came only in later Renaissance art, not from antiquity.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Amor: Latin for 'love', another Roman name for Cupid; spelled backwards it reads 'Roma'.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Kama: The Hindu god of desire, shown with a bow of sugarcane and a string of bees for the bowstring.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Himeros: The Greek personification of sexual desire, one of the winged spirits called Erotes.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Anteros: The god of requited love, a brother of Eros who punished those who scorned love.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Pothos: The Greek personification of longing for someone absent, another of the Erotes.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Hathor: Egyptian goddess of love, music and joy, usually shown with cow horns holding a sun disk.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Ares: The Greek god of war, and sometimes Aphrodite's lover, but he rules battle rather than love.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Mars: The Roman war god, whose lover was Venus, but he is the god of war, not of desire.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Hades: The god of the underworld, who wed Persephone; he presides over the dead, not over romance.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Zeus: The king of the gods, and in Homer Aphrodite's father, but not himself a love deity.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Jupiter: The Roman king of the gods, with a thunderbolt rather than a bow and arrows.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Athena: The goddess of wisdom and strategy, famously a virgin and no patron of romance.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Minerva: The Roman Athena, goddess of wisdom and craft, with no link to love.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Poseidon: The god of the sea and earthquakes, with a trident, not a love deity.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Neptune: The Roman sea god, whose name was given to the planet Neptune, no love deity.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Hermes: Messenger god, and also father of Hermaphroditus with Aphrodite, yet not himself a love deity.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Mercury: The Roman Hermes, whose namesake planet is the fastest in the solar system.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Pluto: Roman underworld god; the dwarf planet Pluto was named in 1930 by an 11-year-old girl.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Saturn: The Roman god of agriculture, whose festival Saturnalia was a time of feasting and gifts.
Gods and spirits of love and desire.Janus: The two-faced Roman god of doorways and beginnings, from whom January takes its name.

Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Hot cross buns: Spiced buns marked with a cross, eaten especially on Good Friday. English tradition once said they never spoiled if baked that day.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Simnel cake: A British fruitcake topped with eleven marzipan balls, standing for the apostles minus Judas.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Pashka: A rich Russian Easter dessert of sweetened cheese, pressed in a pyramid mold and stamped with the letters XB, for Christ is risen.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Kulich: This tall, cylindrical Russian and Ukrainian Easter bread is often iced and is traditionally blessed in church alongside pashka.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Colomba: Italy's dove-shaped Easter cake, topped with almonds and sugar pearls, is the springtime counterpart of Christmas panettone.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Pastiera: A Neapolitan tart of wheat berries, ricotta and orange blossom water, traditionally baked days before Easter to let the flavors mature.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Mazanec: A Czech sweet bread with raisins and almonds, often marked with a cross, baked for Easter Sunday.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Tsoureki: This Greek braided bread is scented with mahleb and mastic, and traditionally holds a dyed red egg, a symbol of Christ's blood and new life.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Chocolate eggs: Chocolate eggs became popular in 19th-century Europe, after improvements in chocolate-making let confectioners mold hollow shapes.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Lamb roast: Lamb is the classic Easter main in many countries, linked to the Paschal lamb of the Passover story.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Creme Egg: Cadbury's Creme Egg has been sold since the 1960s, and the company sells over 200 million of them each year.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Panettone: Christmas bread from Milan, its dome shape and candied fruit signal December in Italy, not Easter.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Pandoro: The star-shaped Verona yeast cake dusted with icing sugar is a Christmas staple in Italy, and its name means golden bread.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Stollen: Dresden's dense Christmas loaf, shaped to resemble swaddled baby Jesus, is packed with dried fruit and marzipan.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Yule log: This rolled sponge cake echoes the old tradition of burning a great log at midwinter, so it is a Christmas treat.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Mince pies: Despite the name, they hold spiced dried fruit, and in Britain eating them in the twelve days of Christmas is said to bring luck.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Christmas pudding: Traditionally made weeks ahead on Stir-up Sunday, and doused in brandy and flamed at the table, it is a Christmas dessert.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Lebkuchen: Spicy German honey cakes from Nuremberg are sold at Christmas markets and may date back to medieval monasteries.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Fruitcake: Fruitcake is a Christmas classic in the English-speaking world, and its alcohol content helps it last for months.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Eggnog: This creamy, spiked winter drink is Christmas-linked, with eggs, milk and nutmeg. Despite the eggs, it is not an Easter food.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Gingerbread man: Said to have been popularized at the court of Elizabeth I, it is a Christmas-season bake.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Candy canes: The cane shape is said to have been created to hang on Christmas trees, though the stories about its origin are unreliable.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Mulled wine: Spiced warm wine is a winter-market classic in Germany, where it is called Gluhwein, and not an Easter dish.
Easter foods (not Christmas ones).Roast goose: Goose was the traditional English Christmas dinner until turkey took over after the 16th century.
